It's a new national standard for teaching the basic subjects... The problem is, it's so completely idiotic that no one understands it and even people with PhDs in Math cannot comprehend their methods for teaching even basic math.

Short Version: A framework for a National Education lesson plan.

Longer Version: Every Child in 2nd grade will learn x,y,z. Every Child in 10 Grade will learn a,b,c. If we do this at a national level then a 5th grader in Boise Idaho can be directly compared to a 5th grader in Orlando, Fl because they are learning the same concepts at the same age.

So why is it so divisive? 2 reasons. (I'm going to use the Maths standards in my examples as I understand it more than the rest of it.)

  1. The standards were written too vaguely. This has led to arguments over what the standard really means when it says, for example, "Students should use appropriate tools strategically." Do you know what that means? How would you add that to a lesson plan?

  2. Parents were not able to help their children with their homework because the parents don't understand the concept being taught because they were never taught it when they were children. Lets say for example the child is given the problem of a "difficult" multiplication like 25 * 30. The parents jump straight into what most people would think of as Normal calculation.

30

x 25

= 750

The lesson, however, was on how to think of complicated problems as a series of simple problems so the lesson says to use the Grid Method which breaks that multiplication into several smaller multiplication and addition steps.

So that same problem becomes: 25 is 10 + 10 + 5 and 30 is 10+10+10 in the Grid Method you make a grid and multiply the row header by the column header and you get this: (tried my best to make a grid, put it in excel to make it pretty)

........10 \ 10 \ 10 \

10 \ 100 \ 100 \ 100 \

10 \ 100 \ 100 \ 100 \

5 \ 50 \ 50 \ 50 \

Add all the Boxes (100 +100 +100 +100 +100 +100 +50 +50 +50) = 750

Is the grid method slower. Yes. But the lesson was about showing that large complicated problems (which the child may think are hard) are really just a series of small problems (which the child probably would think are easy.)

The parent didn't understand that that was the lesson and they never saw the Grid Method before so they have no idea how to complete the problem. Frustrated they complain on Fox News and their mommy blogs that Common Core is horrible.

There is obviously more to it than this but I hope this very brief explanation helps get you started in understanding Common Core.

How is it possible for an economy to exist without something like gold backing up each bank note?

Faith.

For the most part, it's not necessary that a currency have tangible value. It's only necessary that those who exchange it believe that it has, or at least represents, tangible value.

If I wished to pay you in dryer lint, and you were confident that any other person with whom you'd wish to do business would accept that dryer lint as legal tender, then you'd be willing to accept it as payment. It would have value because not only you and I, but any other people you might deal with in the future, simply believe that it does. So long as you can exchange it somewhere down the line for essentially equal value, then it's done its job as a currency, no matter what it actually is and no matter how much or how little innate value it actually has.

The problem is that if the value exists solely because enough people believe that it exists, then simple disbelief in the value destroys the illusion.

And it should be noted that commodity-backed currencies are ultimately only marginally better as far as that goes, since all they really do is move the concept of value back one step, to something that's at least somewhat more consistent. Gold, for instance, has historically been seen to be valuable, but that's really something of a matter of faith as well. If enough people stopped believing that gold was valuable, then it really would lose some notable amount of its value. It's just that, since it's terribly unlikely that people will decide that gold is valueless, it's terribly unlikely that it ever will be valueless, while the same can't be said for a fiat currency.

Even you can do this. Let's say you produce an in-demand product, like ponies. I really want to buy a pony from you. But.. you only accept pony money. Pony money is just worthless sparkle cardboard (sparkleboard), but you'll accept nothing else. This forces me to trade you for pony money. So I give you a leather couch (which has tangible value) for pony money .

This allows you to manipulate the value of pony money in two ways. First, you can raise and lower the price of ponies at will. Second, you can decide what pony money will trade for.

Ordinarily, this sort of system would fail pretty quick, because ponies can be bought elsewhere, and they aren't necessary for day to day life.

Oil, on the other hand, is necessary on a daily basis. So by forcing countries to buy it in dollars, opec has given the US economy a massive bargaining chip with other countries. This is why the US takes a keen interest in countries that attempt to buck the dollar standard and sell oil in gold, or yuan, or rubles.
